imo-1994-01.title: Pair the largest with the smallest
imo-1994-01.body:
Relabel so that $a_1>a_2>\cdots>a_m$.

**Claim.** $a_i+a_{m+1-i}\ge n+1$ for every $i=1,\dots,m$.

*Proof.* Suppose $a_i+a_{m+1-i}\le n$ for some $i$. For each $j=m+1-i,\,m+2-i,\dots,m$ we have $a_j\le a_{m+1-i}$, so
$$a_i<a_i+a_j\le a_i+a_{m+1-i}\le n .$$
By hypothesis each of these $i$ numbers $a_i+a_j$ belongs to the set $\{a_1,\dots,a_m\}$; they are distinct (the $a_j$ are distinct) and all larger than $a_i$. But only $i-1$ elements, $a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}$, are larger than $a_i$ — contradiction. $\square$

**Conclusion.** Summing the claim over $i$,
$$2(a_1+\cdots+a_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m\big(a_i+a_{m+1-i}\big)\ge m(n+1),$$
which is the required inequality. ∎

imo-1994-02.title: Two cyclic quadrilaterals and uniqueness
imo-1994-02.body:
By symmetry in the line $AM$, $OC\perp AC$ and $OB=OC$. In the right triangle $ABO$ (right angle at $B$), $BM\perp AO$, so $M$ is the foot of the altitude from $B$ and lies between $A$ and $O$; hence $\angle OBC=\angle OBM=\angle BAM$, an acute angle, and likewise $\angle OCB=\angle CAM=\angle BAM$. Note $O\notin BC$ and $O\notin AB$.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Assume $OQ\perp EF$.

*Special case $E=B$.* Then line $EF$ is $BC$, so $F=C$, and $OQ\perp BC$ forces $Q=M$, so $QE=QF$. Similarly if $F=C$.

*General case $E\ne B$, $F\ne C$.* Since $\angle OBE=\angle OQE=90^\circ$, the points $B$ and $Q$ lie on the circle with diameter $OE$; so $O,B,E,Q$ are concyclic. The inscribed angles $\angle OEQ$ and $\angle OBQ$ stand on the same chord $OQ$, so they are equal or supplementary. $\angle OEQ$ is acute (triangle $OQE$ has its right angle at $Q$) and $\angle OBQ=\angle OBC$ is acute ($Q$ is on segment $BC$), so $\angle OEQ=\angle OBC$. In the same way ($O,C,F,Q$ concyclic) $\angle OFQ=\angle OCB$. Therefore $\angle OEQ=\angle OFQ$, and in the right triangles $OQE$, $OQF$:
$$QE=OQ\cot\angle OEQ=OQ\cot\angle OFQ=QF .$$

**($\Leftarrow$)** Assume $QE=QF$. Let $\ell$ be the line through $Q$ perpendicular to $OQ$.
- $\ell\not\parallel AB$: otherwise $OQ\perp AB$, so $O,Q,B$ are collinear and $Q=B$ (the line $OB$ meets $BC$ only at $B$). Similarly $\ell\not\parallel AC$. Let $\ell$ meet $AB$ at $E'$ and $AC$ at $F'$.
- $E',Q,F'$ are distinct: $Q\notin AB\cup AC$; and $E'=F'$ would mean $E'=F'=A$, i.e. $AQ\perp OQ$, so $Q$ would lie on the circle with diameter $AO$, which meets line $BC$ only at $B$ and $C$.

By ($\Rightarrow$), $QE'=QF'$. Now there is only one line through $Q$ whose intersections with $AB$ and $AC$ have midpoint $Q$: such an $F$ is the reflection of $E$ in $Q$, so it lies on the reflection of line $AB$ in $Q$, a line parallel to $AB$ that meets $AC$ in exactly one point. Hence $F=F'$, $E=E'$, and $EF=\ell\perp OQ$. ∎

imo-1994-03.title: Steps of $f$ are $0$ or $1$
imo-1994-03.body:
Let $B(x)$ be the number of $1$s in the binary representation of $x$.

**Increment.** Going from $k$ to $k+1$, the set loses $k+1$ and gains $2k+1$ and $2k+2$. Since $B(2k+2)=B(k+1)$, these two cancel, so
$$f(k+1)-f(k)=[B(2k+1)=3]=[B(k)=2]\in\{0,1\},$$
because $2k+1$ is $k$ in binary followed by a $1$.

**(a)** $f(1)=0$ (the set is $\{2\}$), $f$ never decreases, increases by at most $1$ at a time, and increases infinitely often (infinitely many $k$ have $B(k)=2$). So $f$ takes every value $m\ge0$.

**(b)** The set $\{k:f(k)=m\}$ is a block of consecutive integers; it is a single $k$ exactly when $f$ increases both from $k-1$ to $k$ and from $k$ to $k+1$, i.e. when $B(k-1)=B(k)=2$ (with $k\ge2$; $k=1$ gives $f=0$).

If $k$ is odd, $k-1$ is even and $k=(k-1)+1$ has one more $1$ than $k-1$ — impossible. So $k$ is even and $k-1$ is odd with two $1$s: $k-1=2^s+1$, $k=2^s+2$, and $B(k)=2$ requires $s\ge2$.

**Value at $k=2^s+2$.** Count $x\in[2^s+3,\,2^{s+1}+4]$ with $B(x)=3$:
- $x\in[2^s,2^{s+1})$: $x=2^s+y$ with $y<2^s$, $B(y)=2$; there are $\binom s2$ such $x$, the smallest being $2^s+3$, so all are in range.
- $x\in[2^{s+1},2^{s+1}+4]$: $x=2^{s+1}+y$, $y\le4$, $B(y)=2$, only $y=3$.

So $m=f(2^s+2)=\binom s2+1$.

**Answer:** (b) exactly the numbers $m=\binom s2+1$ with $s\ge2$, i.e. $2,4,7,11,16,22,\dots$ ∎

imo-1994-04.title: Symmetry and Vieta-style reduction
imo-1994-04.body:
We need $mn>1$.

**Symmetry.** $\gcd(m,mn-1)=1$ and $m^3(n^3+1)=(mn)^3+m^3\equiv1+m^3\pmod{mn-1}$. So $mn-1\mid n^3+1\iff mn-1\mid m^3+1$, and we may assume $n\ge m$.

**$m=n$.** $\frac{n^3+1}{n^2-1}=\frac{n^2-n+1}{n-1}=n+\frac{1}{n-1}$, an integer only for $n=2$: the pair $(2,2)$ (value $3$).

**$n>m$.** Let $n^3+1=q(mn-1)$ with $q\ge1$. Modulo $n$: $1\equiv-q$, so $q=kn-1$ with $k\ge1$. Expanding $(kn-1)(mn-1)=n^3+1$:
$$kmn^2-(k+m)n=n^3\iff k+m=n(km-n).$$
So $c=km-n$ is a positive integer and $k=cn-m$. Substituting into $c=km-n$:
$$c=(cn-m)m-n\iff n(cm-1)=c+m^2 .$$
Since $n>m$: $c+m^2>m(cm-1)$, i.e. $c(m^2-1)<m^2+m$.
- **$m=1$:** $n(c-1)=c+1$, so $n=1+\frac{2}{c-1}$, giving $n=3$ ($c=2$) or $n=2$ ($c=3$).
- **$m\ge2$:** $c<\frac{m}{m-1}\le2$, so $c=1$ and $n=\frac{m^2+1}{m-1}=m+1+\frac{2}{m-1}$; thus $m\in\{2,3\}$, $n=5$.

Checks: $(1,2)$: $9/1$; $(1,3)$: $28/2$; $(2,5)$: $126/9=14$; $(3,5)$: $126/14=9$.

**Answer:** by symmetry, the pairs are $(2,2),(1,2),(2,1),(1,3),(3,1),(2,5),(5,2),(3,5),(5,3)$. ∎

imo-1994-05.title: Fixed points
imo-1994-05.body:
Write $x*y=x+y+xy=(1+x)(1+y)-1$; this is a commutative, associative operation on $S$. Condition 1 reads $f(x*f(y))=y*f(x)$.

**$f(x)=-\frac{x}{1+x}$ works.** Here $1+f(x)=\frac{1}{1+x}>0$, so $f(x)\in S$. Then $1+x*f(y)=\frac{1+x}{1+y}$, so $1+f(x*f(y))=\frac{1+y}{1+x}$, and also $1+y*f(x)=(1+y)\cdot\frac{1}{1+x}$; condition 1 holds. And $\frac{f(x)}{x}=-\frac{1}{1+x}$ is strictly increasing on $(-1,0)$ and on $(0,\infty)$.

**Uniqueness.** Let $f$ satisfy both conditions.

*Every $u_a=a*f(a)$ is a fixed point:* put $x=y=a$ in condition 1: $f(a*f(a))=a*f(a)$.

*If $u$ is a fixed point, so is $u*u$:* put $x=y=u$: $f(u*f(u))=u*f(u)$, i.e. $f(u*u)=u*u$.

*The only possible fixed point is $0$:* a fixed point $u\ne0$ has $\frac{f(u)}{u}=1$.
- If $u>0$, then $u*u=u^2+2u>u$ is also a fixed point in $(0,\infty)$, so $\frac{f(x)}x$ takes the value $1$ twice on $(0,\infty)$ — contradicting strict monotonicity.
- If $-1<u<0$, then $1+u\in(0,1)$, so $1+u*u=(1+u)^2\in(0,1)$ and $(1+u)^2\ne 1+u$: $u*u$ is another fixed point in $(-1,0)$ — again a contradiction.

Hence $a*f(a)=0$ for every $a\in S$: $(1+a)(1+f(a))=1$, so $f(a)=\frac{1}{1+a}-1=-\frac{a}{1+a}$.

**Answer:** $f(x)=-\dfrac{x}{1+x}$. ∎

imo-1994-06.title: Let the smallest prime factor decide
imo-1994-06.body:
Let $p_1<p_2<p_3<\cdots$ be the primes. Define
$$A=\{\,p_{i_1}p_{i_2}\cdots p_{i_k}\;:\;k\ge2,\ i_1<i_2<\cdots<i_k,\ i_1=k-1\,\},$$
the products of $k\ge2$ distinct primes whose smallest prime factor is the $(k-1)$-th prime. (By unique factorization, membership in $A$ is well defined.)

Let $S=\{q_1<q_2<q_3<\cdots\}$ be any infinite set of primes and let $q_1=p_j$. Put $k=j+1\ge2$.

- $m=q_1q_2\cdots q_k$ is a product of $k$ distinct elements of $S$ and its smallest prime factor is $q_1=p_j=p_{k-1}$, so $m\in A$.
- $n=q_2q_3\cdots q_{k+1}$ is also a product of $k$ distinct elements of $S$, but its smallest prime factor is $q_2=p_{j'}$ with $j'>j=k-1$, so $n\notin A$.

Thus $A$ has the required property. ∎
